content: 1. The transmission of the Ebola virus can occur through bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces (fomites). This was discussed in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2007, volume 196, supplement 2, pages S142-S147. 2. A study by Moreau et al. in 2015, published in Eurosurveillance, highlighted that testing only blood samples using EBOV RT-PCR in lactating mothers infected with the Ebola virus may not be sufficient for accurate diagnosis. 3. Caluwaerts et al. presented two case reports in 2015 in Clinical Infectious Diseases, discussing the complex challenges and dilemmas in managing pregnant women infected with the Ebola virus. 4. Baggi et al. reported on the management of pregnant women infected with the Ebola virus in a treatment center in Guinea in June 2014. This study was published in Eurosurveillance, volume 19, issue 49. 5. Deen et al. published a preliminary report in 2015 in The New England Journal of Medicine, documenting the persistence of Ebola RNA in the semen of male survivors of Ebola virus disease. 6. Mate et al. provided molecular evidence of the sexual transmission of the Ebola virus in a study published in 2015 in The New England Journal of Medicine. 7. Interim guidance documents for the clinical care of Ebola virus disease survivors include tools such as the Patient Health Questionnaire for Depression (PHQ-9) in Appendix I and additional clinical care recommendations in Appendix II.
